concepts.name: Arithmetic patterns
concepts.description: Each term is the previous term plus a fixed difference. Spotting that is the pattern skill; formulas for distant terms and sums belong to Arithmetic Progression.

concepts.name: Geometric patterns
concepts.description: Each term is the previous term times a fixed ratio.

concepts.name: Difference patterns and special sequences
concepts.description: When the differences are not constant, their differences may be. Also know the famous lists: squares, cubes, primes and Fibonacci-style sums.

concepts.name: Finding a missing term
concepts.description: Work out the rule from the terms you have, then apply it to fill the gap.

concepts.name: Alternating and interleaved patterns
concepts.description: Two rules can take turns (+2 then ×2), or the odd-position and even-position terms can form two separate sequences woven together.

concepts.name: Spotting the wrong term
concepts.description: Find the rule that fits almost every term; the one term that breaks it is the wrong number.

formulas.title: Arithmetic pattern
formulas.prompt: How do you spot and continue an arithmetic pattern?
formulas.formula: Each term = previous term + constant difference d
formulas.explanation: Check that the difference between consecutive terms is the same throughout before assuming the pattern is arithmetic.
formulas.commonMistake: Assuming the difference stays constant without checking more than one gap.

formulas.title: Geometric pattern
formulas.prompt: How do you spot and continue a geometric pattern?
formulas.formula: Each term = previous term × constant ratio r
formulas.explanation: Check that consecutive terms share the same ratio, not just the same difference.
formulas.commonMistake: Confusing a geometric pattern with an arithmetic one because the numbers are growing.

formulas.title: Patterns beyond the basics
formulas.prompt: What do you do when a sequence is neither arithmetic nor geometric?
formulas.formula: Look at the differences between terms; if those differences form their own pattern, use it to extend the sequence
formulas.explanation: A constant second difference signals a quadratic-style pattern; the differences themselves grow by a fixed amount each time.
formulas.example: 2, 6, 12, 20, 30: differences are 4, 6, 8, 10, increasing by 2 → next difference 12 → next term 42
formulas.commonMistake: Giving up after checking only whether the sequence is arithmetic or geometric.

formulas.title: Finding a missing term
formulas.prompt: How do you find a term missing from the middle of a sequence?
formulas.formula: Identify the rule from the terms you do have, then apply it forwards (or backwards) to fill the gap
formulas.explanation: Use the surrounding terms on both sides of the gap to confirm the rule before filling it in.
formulas.example: 2, 5, 8, __, 14: difference is 3, so the missing term is 11
formulas.commonMistake: Guessing the missing term without confirming the rule from both directions.

formulas.title: Interleaved sequences
formulas.prompt: What do you check when neither the differences nor the ratios follow a pattern?
formulas.formula: Split the terms into odd positions (1st, 3rd, 5th, …) and even positions (2nd, 4th, …); each half may follow its own rule
formulas.explanation: Two simple sequences woven together look irregular as a whole. Separating them usually reveals two easy patterns.
formulas.example: 1, 10, 3, 20, 5, 30, 7, ?: odd positions 1, 3, 5, 7 and even positions 10, 20, 30, so the next term is 40
formulas.commonMistake: Looking only at consecutive differences (9, −7, 17, −15, …), which hide the two patterns.

formulas.title: Finding the wrong term
formulas.prompt: How do you find the one wrong number in a series?
formulas.formula: Find a rule that fits most consecutive pairs, rebuild the series from the first term, and see which term disagrees
formulas.explanation: One wrong term spoils two differences (the one before it and the one after it), so look for the rule in the pairs that are not affected.
formulas.commonMistake: Blaming the term after the break: 127 looks odd next to 64, but it is 64 that breaks the rule.

formulas.title: Differences of differences
formulas.prompt: The gaps between terms are not equal. What do you try next?
formulas.formula:
Take the differences again.
A constant second difference means a squares pattern.
formulas.explanation: A pattern built on n² grows by steadily increasing steps, so its second differences are constant.
formulas.example: 2, 5, 10, 17, 26: gaps 3, 5, 7, 9 rise by 2, so the next gap is 11 and the next term 37 (n² + 1).
formulas.commonMistake: Guessing a ratio because the numbers grow quickly.

formulas.title: Look next to squares and cubes
formulas.prompt: Terms seem irregular but close to familiar numbers. What do you check?
formulas.formula:
Compare each term with n², n³ or n² ± n:
0, 7, 26, 63 = n³ − 1
2, 9, 28, 65 = n³ + 1
3, 8, 15, 24 = n² − 1
formulas.explanation: Many series are perfect squares or cubes shifted by a small constant.
formulas.example: 3, 8, 15, 24, 35 are 2² − 1 to 6² − 1, so the next is 7² − 1 = 48.
formulas.commonMistake: Starting n at 1 when the pattern starts at 2.

levels.title: Finding the Rule
levels.description: Spotting whether a sequence adds, multiplies, or follows a more complex pattern.

blocks.title: Two basic patterns
blocks.body: A sequence like 5, 9, 13, 17 adds the same amount each time (arithmetic). A sequence like 3, 6, 12, 24 multiplies by the same amount each time (geometric). Checking a difference and a ratio quickly tells you which one you have.

blocks.title: Arithmetic vs geometric
blocks.body:
Arithmetic: term + d
Geometric: term × r
blocks.caption: Check whether consecutive terms share a constant difference or a constant ratio.

blocks.body: If the differences are not constant, check the ratios next — and if neither works, look at the differences of the differences.
Later levels add two more tricks: series where two patterns take turns or are woven together, and series with one wrong number to find.

levels.title: Sequences Formulas
levels.description: Differences, ratios, special sequences, interleaved patterns, missing terms and wrong terms.

levels.title: Direct Patterns
levels.description: Continuing arithmetic and geometric sequences, and filling simple gaps.

levels.title: Beyond the Basics
levels.description: Second differences, famous sequences, alternating rules and a first wrong-term hunt.

levels.title: Multi-Layer Patterns
levels.description: Layered differences, interleaved sequences and wrong terms that hide their neighbours.

questions.question: What comes next: 5, 9, 13, 17, ?
questions.explanation: The difference between consecutive terms is 4, so the next term is 17 + 4 = 21.
questions.method: Find the constant difference, then add it once more.

hints.text: Check the gap between each pair of consecutive terms.

commonMistakes: Using the wrong difference by checking only one gap.

questions.question: What comes next: 3, 6, 12, 24, ?
questions.explanation: Each term doubles, so the next term is 24 × 2 = 48.
questions.method: Find the constant ratio, then multiply once more.

hints.text: Check what each term is multiplied by to get the next.

commonMistakes: Treating this as an arithmetic pattern and adding a fixed amount.

questions.question: What is the missing term: 2, 5, 8, __, 14?
questions.method: Confirm the rule using the terms before and after the gap.

hints.text: Check the difference between 8 and 14 spans two steps.

commonMistakes: Guessing a value without checking it against both neighbours.

questions.question: The sequence 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 is best described as
questions.explanation: Each term is double the one before it (a constant ratio of 2), which makes it geometric, not arithmetic.

hints.text: The differences (2, 4, 8, 16) are not constant, but the ratios are.

commonMistakes: Assuming a growing sequence must be arithmetic.

questions.question: What comes next: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ?
questions.explanation: These are perfect squares: 1², 2², 3², 4², 5², so the next term is 6² = 36.

hints.text: Compare each term to the square of its position.

commonMistakes: Trying to find a constant difference, which does not exist here.

questions.question: What comes next: 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ?
questions.explanation: The differences are 4, 6, 8, 10, increasing by 2 each time. The next difference is 12, so the next term is 30 + 12 = 42.
questions.method: Look at the differences between terms.

hints.text: The differences themselves form an arithmetic pattern.

commonMistakes: Assuming the sequence itself is arithmetic.

questions.question: What comes next: 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ?
questions.explanation: Each term is the sum of the two before it: 8 + 13 = 21.
questions.method: Check whether each term is built from the two before it.

hints.text: Try adding the two previous terms.

commonMistakes: Looking only for a constant difference or ratio.

questions.question: The sequence alternates +2 and ×2: 3, 5, 10, 12, 24, 26, ?. What comes next?
questions.method: Track which operation applies at each step.

hints.text: The operations alternate: +2, then ×2, then +2, then ×2, …

commonMistakes: Applying +2 instead of ×2 at this step.

questions.question: What is the missing term: 4, __, 36, 108?
questions.explanation: Each term is 3 times the one before it (ratio 3), so the missing term is 4 × 3 = 12. Check: 12 × 3 = 36. ✓
solutionSteps: 108 ÷ 36 = 3, so each term is 3 times the one before.
questions.method: Find the ratio using the terms you know, then apply it.

hints.text: This is a geometric pattern, not arithmetic.

commonMistakes: Trying a constant-difference rule instead of a constant ratio.

questions.question: What comes next: 1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, ?
questions.explanation: The differences are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, increasing by 1 each time. The next difference is 6, so the next term is 16 + 6 = 22.
questions.method: The differences themselves increase by a constant amount.

hints.text: Check the differences of the differences.

questions.question: Continuing the alternating +2, ×2 pattern 3, 5, 10, 12, 24, 26, 52, 54, …, what is the 9th term?
questions.explanation: The steps alternate +2, ×2: 3, 5, 10, 12, 24, 26, 52, 54. The 8th term came from a +2 step, so the 9th uses ×2: 54 × 2 = 108.
questions.method: Track the operation for each step carefully, especially near the end.

hints.text: List enough terms to be sure which operation comes next.

commonMistakes: Applying +2 instead of ×2 at the 9th step.

questions.question: What comes next: 1, 10, 3, 20, 5, 30, 7, ?
questions.explanation: Two sequences are woven together. Odd positions: 1, 3, 5, 7 (adding 2). Even positions: 10, 20, 30 (adding 10). The next term is in an even position, so it is 30 + 10 = 40.
solutionSteps: The 8th term is an even position: 40.
questions.method: Split the series into odd and even positions.

hints.text: The terms jump up and down. Try reading every other term.
Which of the two sequences does the next term belong to?

commonMistakes: Continuing the odd-position sequence and giving 9.

questions.question: Which number is wrong in the series 1, 8, 27, 64, 124, 216?
questions.explanation: The terms are cubes: 1³, 2³, 3³, 4³, 5³, 6³. But 5³ = 125, not 124, so 124 is the wrong number.
questions.method: Recognise the special sequence, then check each term against it.

hints.text: These numbers grow fast. Are they powers of something?
What is 5 × 5 × 5?

commonMistakes: Choosing 216 because the jump from 124 to 216 looks large.

questions.question: What comes next: 2, 3, 4, 9, 8, 27, 16, ?
questions.explanation: Odd positions: 2, 4, 8, 16 (doubling). Even positions: 3, 9, 27 (multiplying by 3). The next term is in an even position: 27 × 3 = 81.
questions.method: Split into two sequences and find each one's rule.

hints.text: Read every other term, starting from 2.
Now read every other term starting from 3.

commonMistakes: Giving 32 by continuing the doubling sequence, which is not next.

questions.question: Which number is wrong in the series 3, 7, 15, 31, 64, 127?
questions.explanation: Each term is double the previous term plus 1: 3 → 7 → 15 → 31 → 63 → 127. The series shows 64 instead of 63, so 64 is wrong. With 63, the last step 63 × 2 + 1 = 127 also fits.
questions.method: Find the rule from the unaffected pairs, then rebuild the series.

hints.text: Compare each term with double the previous one.
Which term is not 1 more than double the one before?

commonMistakes: Choosing 127, which only looks wrong because it follows the wrong term.

questions.question: Which number is wrong in the series 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, 44, 56?
questions.explanation: The differences should be 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14: each term is n(n + 1). So the sixth term is 30 + 12 = 42 = 6 × 7, not 44. Then 42 + 14 = 56 fits.
questions.method: Use the difference pattern from the unaffected terms.

hints.text: Write down the differences between terms.
The differences should rise by 2 each time. Where does that break?

commonMistakes: Choosing 56, whose difference from 44 (12) looks out of place only because 44 is wrong.
